title: How ‘Reading Instruction’ Fails Black And Brown Children
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Natalie Wexler argues that the standard approach to elementary reading instruction is an injustice that falls hardest on black, Hispanic and low-income children. She opens with national reading proficiency figures showing large racial gaps and a downward trend, then says the scientific evidence on why the approach fails is widely ignored. What works, she says, is systematic phonics together with early knowledge-building, whereas schools give phonics a token nod, encourage guessing at words and sideline social studies and science for illusory comprehension skills. She illustrates the damage with an imagined fourth-grader stuck in leveled reading, practising skills on easy texts, and concluding the fault is their own. She contrasts this with a second-grade class, black and brown and low-income, engaged by a content-rich curriculum on Ancient India, Greek mythology and the Civil War.
points: Reading outcomes for black students are low and falling, and Wexler frames the research-practice gap as a social justice failure that education can address.
The effective combination is systematic phonics plus early knowledge-building, not token phonics plus comprehension-skill drills.
Leveled reading works as a form of tracking with no evidence it boosts comprehension, and it can teach children they are bad readers.
A content-rich curriculum engaged low-income children and gave them vocabulary and knowledge as a foundation for high school.
quotes: On national tests last year, only 18 percent of black 4th-graders scored proficient or above in reading; the figure for white 4th-graders was 45 percent.

There’s abundant scientific evidence that explains why our standard approach to reading instruction isn’t working for so many black kids—and others. But educators and policymakers are often unaware of that research; some reject it.

They are powerful. But there’s much more that education can do, right now, for our most vulnerable children that we simply haven’t tried. When it comes to reading, what works is a simultaneous mix of two things at early grade levels: systematic instruction in phonics, and starting to build the kind of knowledge students will need in high school and beyond.

Those children were lucky enough to attend a school using an atypical elementary curriculum focused on meaty content: Ancient India, Greek mythology, the human digestive system, the War of 1812—and the Civil War, slavery, and civil rights heroes. They were deeply engaged in the material and proud of all they were learning. And the knowledge and vocabulary they were acquiring—words like labyrinth and plummeted—would provide a foundation for their success in high school and beyond.

It’s not. There’s no evidence that leveled reading boosts comprehension. And given stagnant or declining reading scores, there’s plenty of evidence it doesn’t. But kids don’t know that. In addition to depriving them—and us—of the opportunity to live up to their potential, this system is making untold numbers of them feel like failures for no good reason.

Well-intentioned as it may be, the prevailing approach to literacy is failing millions of children who are disproportionately black and brown. If people truly understood the needless damage being done by our schools every day, they would be out in the streets demanding change.
